acts.title: Text A · The first winter
text: People automatically assume that I must find it difficult, and they are considerably wrong.

In Tromsø we have what is called a polar night, when the sun basically does not appear for twenty-four hours. It goes on for sixty days. Said aloud it sounds thoroughly depressing, and my first November here was genuinely hard.

What changed was noticing what everybody else did. They did not stay indoors being cosy. They wrapped up warm and went out — skiing, walking, playing in the snow under artificial light, which sounds bleak and is not.

From November to February the town is full of light precisely because there is none. People decorate their houses obsessively, and the streets are lit with candles. The effect is genuinely magical, and I have stopped apologizing for the word.

items.q: What does the writer say about people’s assumptions?
o: People assume it must be difficult, and they are wrong

items.q: What changed the writer’s mind about the polar night?
o: Noticing that everybody went outside anyway

acts.title: Text B · The white nights, and the choice
text: The other half of the year is stranger. For sixty days the sun never really sets: it only gets slightly darker for about an hour in the middle of the night.

People behave accordingly. The nights are as lively as the days, and outdoor concerts start at times that would be absurd anywhere else. The only real downside is that sleeping becomes surprisingly difficult, although nobody complains about it very seriously.

My homeland is considerably warmer than Norway, and there the sun rises and sets at almost exactly the same time all year. We have seasons — dry and cool, then hot and wet — but the change is far less dramatic.
If I had to choose, I would probably take the dark. I still get ridiculously excited about snow, and it looks extraordinarily beautiful under the streetlamps.

items.s: For sixty days the sun does not fully set.
It gets completely dark for an hour in the middle of the night.
People complain seriously about the difficulty of sleeping.
The writer’s homeland has almost no variation in sunrise times.
Given the choice, the writer prefers the summer.

items.q: “People automatically assume…” — what does the adverb describe?
o: How they assume it — the manner of the verb

items.q: “considerably warmer” — what does the adverb describe here?
o: The adjective warmer — it says by how much

items.q: “I still get ridiculously excited.” Where is the adverb?
o: In front of the adjective it modifies

items.q: Which adverb does NOT end in -ly in these sentences?

acts.title: Adjectives, adverbs, and where they stand
rule: An adjective describes a thing. An adverb describes almost everything else: how a verb happens, how much an adjective applies, or the writer’s attitude to the whole sentence. Most adverbs are built with -ly, and the ones that are not are the ones learners get wrong.
points: Add -ly. If the adjective ends in -y, change to -ily: easy → easily. If it ends in -le, drop the e: gentle → gently. If it ends in -ic, add -ally: automatic → automatically.
good → well. fast, hard, late, early keep the same form. hardly and lately exist, and mean something else entirely.
Usually after the verb or after the object: She speaks Norwegian fluently. Never between verb and object.
In front of the word they modify: considerably warmer, ridiculously excited, far less dramatic.
Before the main verb but after be: I always wrap up. It is always cold.
At the front, with a comma: Honestly, I prefer the dark.
eg: She speaks Norwegian fluently.
Manner — after the object, not before it.
She speaks Russian well and Norwegian fluently.
Two adverbs of manner, each after its own object.
My homeland is considerably warmer.
Degree, in front of the comparative.
It only gets slightly darker.
Degree.
People automatically assume it is difficult.
Manner, before the main verb — common with automatically.
I always wrap up warm.
Frequency, before the main verb.
It is always cold in February.
Frequency, after be.
Honestly, I prefer the dark.
Comment adverb, front position.
He works hard. He hardly works.
Same word, opposite meanings. hardly = almost not.
She arrived late. I haven’t seen her lately.
late = not on time. lately = recently.
acts.careful: Two traps. First, never put an adverb of manner between a verb and its object: “She speaks fluently Norwegian” is wrong. Second, hard / hardly and late / lately are not adjective-and-adverb pairs — “He hardly works” means he does almost nothing, which is the opposite of what a learner usually intends.

write.q: Write about 180 words on the climate where you live and what people actually do about it — not what outsiders imagine. Use at least four adverbs of degree in front of adjectives, at least two adverbs of manner in the right position, and one comment adverb at the front of a sentence.
plan: what the winter or summer is really like
write.model:
People automatically assume that a Karaganda winter is unbearable, and they are considerably wrong about which part of it is hard.

The cold itself is manageable. Minus thirty is a dry cold, and everybody dresses for it properly from about the age of four. What is genuinely difficult is February, when it has been dark at four in the afternoon for three months and the snow has stopped being white.

What people do about it is not what visitors expect. Nobody stays indoors. The skating rinks are full at nine in the evening, the banya is busier in January than in June, and children play outside in weather that would close a school in London.

Honestly, I prefer it to the summer. July here is only slightly less extreme in the other direction, and there is nothing you can put on to make forty degrees comfortable. You can always add a coat.
